requirement:
> `Close a delivered search and record dependencies for snippets you used to
> justify your conclusion without an additional source read. search_id is the
> result's UUID and used is an array of its short entry tags, e.g.
> {"search_id":"11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111","used":["1"]}. Entries
> whose source you also read may be omitted; including them is harmless. Use
> used:[] when no entries qualify, including an empty search. Every delivered
> search must be finished before submission. The result is {search_id,
> finished:true}; no additional source is delivered.`
rationale:
structural: The subject text is the literal MCP description string for `finish_search`. It states no library, algorithm, signature, type, field, or delegation through a named interface. The only candidate obligation is that the advertised tool description reads exactly as quoted. A behavior-preserving alternative, such as building the string from a constant or in another module, still yields the same description, so where the string lives is discretionary. The prose about used tags, `used:[]`, and finishing every search describes how a model should use the tool. It doesn't prescribe how the code is built. Nothing in the text needs implementation evidence beyond the emitted string.

The supplied root, `crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/project_sources.rs#impl[Session<'_, D>/ToolSession<D>]/fn[definitions]`, does produce the `FINISH_SEARCH` definition. Its description string matches the requirement text, and its parameters are `search_id` and `used`. So the root supports the requirement, and no marker is missing.

behavioral: The requirement `requirements.sdk.graph.search.finish_search.mcp.description` states one observable obligation. The published `finish_search` tool description must be the quoted text. The test `crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/project_sources.rs#mod[tests]/fn[published_tool_descriptions_match_the_contract]` carries a `{test}` reference to it. It builds `ProjectSources`, gets the published definitions from `tools.session().definitions()`, and finds the `finish_search` definition. It then uses `assert_eq!` to compare that definition's `description` with the full expected string. I compared the expected string with the requirement's quoted text, with the lines joined by single spaces. They match word for word. That covers the example JSON, the note that entries you also read may be omitted, `used:[]`, the rule that every search must be finished, and the `{search_id, finished:true}` result. An exact equality assertion would fail on any change to the text. No other behavioral obligation needs a test.
